newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea shrugs off "boat people" warnings.
newsitem.headline: South Korea shrugs off "boat people" warnings.

text.p: South Korean officials on Tuesday shrugged off fears of an influx of North Korean "boat people" after two families completed what could be the first direct sea escape to the South.
Officials from the National Unification Ministry, responsible for inter-Korean matters, said all future "boat people" from the communist North would be accepted.
"We don't foresee an imminent collapse of North Korea but we are fully prepared for any possibility," said Lee Jong-riol, director-general at the ministry's Humanitarian Bureau.
"We have an emergency plan to cope with a mass influx of refugees," he said.
Before dawn on Tuesday, 14 North Koreans belonging to two families arrived in the South Korean port of Inchon after being picked up from a wooden craft used for their dash south.

The daring direct sea escape and growing number of defections made in large groups in recent months set off alarm bells in Seoul that the North's deteriorating food and economic situation might soon become so dire that there would be a mass influx of refugees.
In December, a family of 16 and a security guard flew into South Korea after a six-week journey via China and Hong Kong.
"Is this a signal for a mass exodus by sea?" asked the Dong-A Ilbo newspaper.
"This presages that North Korea's borders and coast lines will all turn into exit routes," said another influential daily, the Chosun Ilbo.

Lee at the unification ministry said the 1997 state budget called for the construction of a vocational training centre to process defectors from the North but brushed aside as "rash speculation" suggestion of an imminent mass influx of refugees.

"We are still looking for a site to build the centre which is due to be completed by November next year with an initial capacity to handle 100 refugees, although it could be built in a way to be expanded quickly to accommodate 500 people," he said.
"In an unlikely event of a sudden exodus of North Koreans, emergency arrangements would be made, utilising abandoned school facilities to hold refugees," Lee added.
Kim Koo-seup, chief researcher on North Korea at the state-backed Korea Institute of Defence Analysis, said a growing number of defections were motivated by economic reasons.

A U.N. aid official likened famine in the North to a time bomb. Aid officials talk of peasants scrounging for tree bark, wild grass and edible roots. Pyongyang authorities have said children are dying of malnutrition.
Seoul government officials said between 40 and 50 North Koreans had defected annually since 1994, against less than 10 each year before then.
"In less than five months this year, a total of 41 North Koreans defected to the South," Lee said. "We expect the number to grow at a faster pace."
But Kim cautioned against drawing parallels with East Germany at the time of the collapse of communism when there was a flight of people to West Germany.

"The seaborne escape by two families will certainly make North Korea tighten security along its coasts as it tighened security along the border with China, which has become a jump-off point," he said.
"North Korea is a garrison state, citizens are tightly controlled and boats are not easily available," he added.
